video_title: A Historic El Niño Is Coming That Could Cost the World Trillions | Odd Lots
gist: Dartmouth climate scientist Justin Mankin tells Odd Lots that forecasting models are converging on a record El Niño — one the Australian Bureau of Meteorology's relative Niño index puts above a 3.3 threshold never previously reached — and that his causal-inference work shows El Niño depresses the growth rate rather than the level of GDP, so losses compound indefinitely. He estimates roughly $10 trillion of global economic losses over the next five years conservatively, up to $14 trillion including tails, and argues there is little evidence humanity is well adapted even to a phenomenon it has experienced for centuries.

themes.theme: The record forecast and its timing

insights.claim: Every current forecast — both statistical and process-based physical models — is converging on an El Niño warmer than the 2015-16 event, making it the strongest at least since 1950 and arguably comparable only to the 1877-78 event.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Model convergence across independent methodologies is the strongest form of this signal — this is a forecastable macro shock, not a tail risk, and it has a known seasonal calendar.

insights.claim: The Australian Bureau of Meteorology's relative oceanic Niño index is projecting a 3.3 threshold that has never been reached in the record, putting this event out of sample.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Out-of-sample means historical analogues understate impacts — any El Niño playbook built on 1997-98 or 2015-16 is a floor, not a central case.

insights.claim: An El Niño advisory has been in effect since June, the event typically peaks in December-January-February, and Mankin expects the wind-down in February-March 2027 — so impacts run across two calendar years.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: A dated event window for positioning: peak physical disruption in DJF, with agricultural and inflation consequences persisting through 2027.

insights.claim: The El Niño has already delayed the onset of the South Asian monsoon, which Mankin links through a causal chain to farmer irrigation demand, Indian diesel prices and subsidy politics — impacts that are manifesting now rather than at the winter peak.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: A tradeable second-order chain already in motion: delayed monsoon raises Indian diesel demand and fiscal subsidy pressure, with knock-on effects for the rupee and Indian rates.

insights.claim: 2026 has a non-trivial chance of being the warmest year on record because of this El Niño on top of the warming trend, and a record 2027 temperature is described as nearly locked in before the year has unfolded.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Record-temperature years are a forecastable input to cooling demand, crop stress and catastrophe-insurance loss ratios for the next two years.

insights.claim: Sell-side research has already begun pricing the event: Tracy Alloway cites a Citi note on Thai interest rates calling it inflationary, a Morgan Stanley Bank of England outlook, and a Bank of America FX outlook on EM currencies all referencing El Niño.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Weather appearing in rates and FX research is itself the signal that this is entering market pricing — the early-mover window is narrowing.

themes.theme: Growth-rate damage, not a level shock

insights.claim: Mankin and Chris Callahan's 2023 Science paper found El Niño does not cause a level effect you recover from — it systematically shifts a country onto a lower growth trajectory, so losses accrue indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Overturns the standard treatment of weather as a transitory shock; if right, El Niño years deserve permanent downward revisions to trend growth in exposed economies rather than a one-quarter haircut.
insights.quote: El Niño seems to systematically depress growth, meaning your country is growing at a rate, and then an El Niño occurs, and then you are growing on a different trajectory.

insights.claim: The 1997-98 El Niño was estimated at about $36 billion in losses at the time as a level shock, but growth accounting five years out puts the true figure at about $5.7 trillion by 2003 — a difference of more than two orders of magnitude.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: The most striking number in the episode: conventional damage estimates for weather events may understate true economic cost by 100x, which reprices climate risk across insurance, sovereign credit and infrastructure.

insights.claim: Using a perfect-model framework, the researchers found the data record is not long enough to recover a known permanent effect even if one exists — meaning they cannot rule out that El Niño's economic impacts are permanent.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: An honest statement of the identification limit — but it means the $10 trillion estimate is a lower bound constrained by data length, not by physics.

insights.claim: Mankin's estimate for the forthcoming event is roughly $10 trillion in global economic losses over five years conservatively, up to $14 trillion including tail effects, with only about 70% of that supported by in-sample historical data.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: A headline number to test against consensus GDP forecasts — if even partly right, growth expectations for El Niño-exposed EM economies through 2030 are too high.
insights.quote: I estimate somewhere around $10 trillion of global economic losses conservatively, over the next five years, right up to $14 trillion of economic losses if you take some of these tail

insights.claim: The loss estimate scales with the size of the global economy as well as the magnitude of the event — a bigger economy simply has more stuff to be impacted — which is why this event's absolute cost dwarfs prior ones.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Implies rising absolute climate losses even with constant hazard frequency — the denominator effect that makes historical loss ratios misleading for insurers.

insights.claim: The identified mechanism for permanent damage is global simultaneity: El Niño generates heat waves, droughts, floods, landslides and wildfires in many disparate regions at once, so it is not one supply-chain disruption but a dozen, degrading where capital can be invested and how efficiently labor and capital are mobilized.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Explains why diversification fails for this risk class — correlated global hazards are precisely what portfolio diversification cannot hedge, which is also the core analogy to global warming.

insights.claim: El Niño's economic damage scales with teleconnection strength — countries whose weather is most tightly physically coupled to the phenomenon suffer the largest negative growth deviations, with Peru's road washouts disrupting mine-to-port commodity flows as the worked example.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Gives a screen for country exposure: rank EM economies by teleconnection strength rather than by headline commodity dependence to find the mispriced sovereigns and miners.

insights.claim: The identification strategy treats El Niño as effectively randomly assigned — the global economy does not influence tropical Pacific sea surface temperatures — making it a natural experiment analogous to a randomized medical trial despite being cyclical.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: This exogeneity is why the growth-depression finding is credible where most climate-damage estimates are not — a template for identifying causal macro effects of physical shocks.

insights.claim: Mankin's blunt conclusion is that the sheer size of documented El Niño losses, after centuries of exposure to the phenomenon, is itself evidence that societies are not optimally adapted to the climate they already have.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Undercuts the standard 'adaptation will handle it' assumption in long-run climate-economic models — a reason to discount the resilience premium built into infrastructure and insurance valuations.
insights.quote: There isn't a whole lot of evidence that we're well adapted to the climate we have.

insights.claim: Mankin separates two distinct adaptation problems that are usually conflated: making global markets resilient so weather shocks don't transmit into prices and interest rates, versus protecting individuals from proximate physical hazards — which require entirely different tools.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Clarifies where investable adaptation actually lies: early warning systems, emergency management and hazard-aware insurance products, versus macro resilience which is a policy problem.

insights.claim: Forecast lead time is itself the adaptation technology — the 1982-83 event arrived without much warning, whereas today's forecasts allow resources to be pre-positioned, which is why financial planners incorporating El Niño into market and supply-chain views is a form of resilience building.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Positions weather-forecast capability as economically valuable infrastructure — and suggests capital that acts on the forecast early captures the adaptation premium.

insights.claim: Because background global warming has raised tropical Pacific baseline temperatures, the relative Niño index uses a rolling baseline — and that secular warming is what makes this El Niño genuinely out of sample rather than merely large.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: The interaction term matters more than either factor alone: warming plus a strong El Niño produces conditions with no historical analogue, so risk models calibrated on history will fail.

insights.claim: El Niño has 'flavors' — the spatial pattern of sea surface temperature anomalies across the Niño 3, Niño 4 and Niño 3.4 regions differs by event and determines which hazards appear where, including Atlantic hurricane occurrence.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: Warns against a single generic El Niño trade — the regional impact map depends on the spatial pattern, so the specific index readings matter for which commodities and insurers are hit.

insights.claim: Mankin argues the climate system is endogenous to economic growth in both directions — emissions from growth alter climate, and climate variability has a finger on the scale of economic output — which he says policy frameworks fail to represent.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: A two-way feedback means damage functions in integrated assessment models — the basis of most climate policy cost-benefit analysis — systematically understate costs.

insights.claim: El Niño is the collapse of the easterly trade winds that normally pile warm water into the West Pacific warm pool near Indonesia and Australia, releasing that heat across the whole tropical Pacific — Mankin's analogy is moving from a corner space heater to wall-to-wall radiators.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: The clearest available mental model for why El Niño reconfigures global weather rather than shifting one region — it changes how much of the atmosphere is exposed to ocean heat.

insights.claim: Peruvian potato farmers were forecasting El Niño as long as 500 years ago by observing reduced visibility of the Pleiades caused by high cirrus cloud shields over the Andes, and adjusting their planting dates accordingly.
insights.speaker: Justin Mankin (Dartmouth)
insights.so_what: A striking counterpoint that predictive adaptation is centuries old — and that the modern failure is institutional rather than informational.

insights.claim: The 1877-78 El Niño is documented in Mike Davis's 'Late Victorian Holocausts' as causing famines in India, northern China and northeastern Brazil — evidence that a single event can reshape political and economic trajectories for generations.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal and Justin Mankin
insights.so_what: The historical precedent for treating a single El Niño as a regime event rather than a weather season — which is precisely the permanent-growth-damage thesis in narrative form.

insights.claim: Alloway closes by noting the El Niño arrives against a backdrop of higher fertilizer prices and constrained supply, with something like 30-40% of global fertilizer supply stuck in the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: The compounding trade: a record agricultural weather shock landing simultaneously with a fertilizer supply squeeze is a far stronger case for agricultural commodity upside than either alone.
